title: A Federal Judge Just Told USCIS It Cannot Freeze Benefits for 39 Countries. India Is on the List.
excerpt: A 135-page ruling calls the Trump administration's immigration freeze 'arbitrary and capricious,' unblocking thousands of pending applications for Indian workers and families
body:
A federal judge in Rhode Island has struck down a Trump administration policy that froze immigration benefits for people from 39 countries — a sweeping ruling that could immediately unblock thousands of pending asylum, work permit, green card, and citizenship applications, including those filed by Indian nationals.

Chief U.S. District Judge John McConnell Jr. issued a 135-page opinion on Friday calling the policies "contrary to law and arbitrary and capricious." He accused U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services of exceeding its authority, failing to provide reasoned explanations, and using "pretextual concerns of 'national security' that mask anti-immigrant sentiments."

"USCIS's hold on adjudications cannot be attributed to anything that these individuals did wrong," McConnell wrote. "Rather, it arises solely by the happenstance of their birth."

## The Backstory

The administration enacted the freeze last winter after the fatal shooting of a National Guard member in Washington, D.C. An Afghan national who had been granted asylum was charged with first-degree murder. In the shooting's aftermath, Trump called for a "permanent pause" on migration from "all Third World Countries."

USCIS responded by halting the processing of immigration benefits — asylum, work permits, green cards, citizenship — for applicants from 39 African, Asian, Latin American, and Middle Eastern countries. The agency also ordered a retroactive review of benefits already granted to anyone from those countries who entered the U.S. during the Biden administration.

The freeze affected people who had followed every step of the legal immigration process. Many lost jobs or legal status while waiting. Families postponed education, travel, and homeownership because their cases sat in limbo without explanation.

## What the Ruling Means for Indian Immigrants

India is among the Asian countries whose nationals have been caught in the freeze. For the tens of thousands of Indian workers on H-1B visas navigating the labyrinthine path to permanent residency, any delay at USCIS can cascade through their entire immigration timeline — affecting employment authorization renewals, green card priority dates, and family petitions.

The ruling applies broadly to all pending USCIS cases involving people from the affected countries, not just the specific plaintiffs who sued, according to the American Immigration Lawyers Association.

"It is an important legal victory to ensure that legal immigration pathways remain open and that USCIS is held accountable to doing their congressionally mandated job of adjudicating applications," said Shev Dalal-Dheini, AILA's senior director of government relations.

## The Government's Defence

In its motion to dismiss — which the court denied — the government argued that Congress gave the executive branch broad authority over immigration policy, including "discretion within the statutory scheme to confer as well as withdraw various discretionary benefits."

DHS general counsel James Percival called the animus claims "a gambit from the Left," but the court disagreed. McConnell wrote that the policies "placed the lives of countless individuals on hold — solely by virtue of their countries of birth."

## The Wider Pattern

The ruling is part of a broader judicial pushback against the administration's immigration crackdown. Earlier this week, a separate federal judge struck down Trump's efforts to bar immigrants from 39 countries from receiving decisions on various immigration applications.

The Supreme Court, meanwhile, is expected to rule by the end of June on Trump's attempt to end birthright citizenship — a case that could further reshape the landscape for immigrant families, particularly the more than 300,000 Indian skilled workers waiting for green cards whose U.S.-born children's citizenship could be affected.

Democracy Forward president Skye Perryman, whose group represented the plaintiffs, called the ruling "a basic principle: the federal government cannot shut down lawful immigration pathways or discriminate against people based on where they come from."

For the Indian diaspora navigating America's increasingly hostile immigration system, it is a rare courtroom win. Whether it holds on appeal is the next question.

*Sources: Reuters, Associated Press, Wall Street Journal, American Immigration Lawyers Association*
